parsed_reason_text: July 11, 2025 Dr. Cathy Sandeen President California State University East Bay 25800 Carlos Bee Blvd Hayward, CA 94542-3011 Dear President Sandeen: This letter serves as formal notification and official record of action taken concerning California State University East Bay (CSUEB) by the WASC Senior College and University Commission (WSCUC) at its meeting June 27, 2025. At that meeting the Commission decided to place CSUEB on Notice of Concern. This action was taken after consideration of the report of the review team that conducted the accreditation Visit to CSUEB March 19-21, 2025 using the 2023 Standards of accreditation. The Commission also reviewed the institutional report and exhibits submitted by CSUEB prior to the Offsite Review (OSR), the supplemental materials requested by the team after the OSR, and the institution’s May 23, 2025 response to the team report. The Commission appreciated the opportunity to discuss the visit with you and your colleagues Fanny Yeung, Associate Vice President Institutional Strategy and Effectiveness; Kathleen Wong Lau, University Diversity Officer; Brenda Amenson-Hill, Vice President of Student Affairs; Myeshia Armstrong, Vice President Administration and Finance and Chief financial Officer; Jenny O, Academic Senate Chair; Monique Cornelius, Associate Vice Provost Budget and Planning; Rafael Hernandez, Associate Provost; Silvina Ituarte, Associate Provost; and Kim Greer, Provost and Vice President Academic Affairs. Your comments were very helpful in informing the Commission’s deliberations. The date of this action constitutes the effective date of the institution’s new status with WSCUC. Actions 1. Receive the accreditation Visit team report 2. Reaffirm accreditation for a period of six years 3. Issue a Notice of Concern 4. Schedule the next reaffirmation review with the Offsite Review in fall 2030 and the accreditation Visit in spring 2031 5. Schedule a Special Visit in fall 2027 addressing Standard 3, CFRs 3.4 and 3.5 and all requirements in this letter Commendations The Commission commends the institution for: 1. Mission alignment to regional economic health, support for student populations, access for non-traditional students, large numbers of transfer students, and contributions to the public good. 2. Progress of Institutional Effectiveness and Research (IER) in enhancing quality assurance processes across the university by enabling the campus to analyze retention rates and graduation at the institutional, program, and course levels. 3. Commitment to upward social and economic mobility, as demonstrated by the high ranking in the California Mobility Index. Notice of Concern A Notice of Concern provides notice to the institution that, while it currently meets WSCUC Standards, it is in danger of being found out of compliance with one or more Standards if current trends or findings continue. Institutions issued a Notice of Concern are scheduled for a Special Visit. If the issues are not addressed, a sanction could be imposed as described in the 2023 Handbook of accreditation. A Notice of Concern is public information and will be posted on the WSCUC website. Standards at Risk of Non-Compliance and Requiring a Response Standard 3, CFR 3.4 Resource Planning and CFR 3.5 Fiscal Stability: 1. Develop, communicate, and implement budgetary plans in collaboration with stakeholders to ensure financial stability and long-term sustainability. 2. Develop a comprehensive strategic enrollment plan that includes multiple budget scenarios and options for financial sustainability including scenarios that reflect risks and uncertainties for the institution. 3. Assess the return on investment of existing enrollment management initiatives. 4. Align current and future distance education offerings with objectives for enrollment and revenue growth. Areas for Development The Commission also requires the institution to respond to the following areas for development: 1. Redevelop the academic program review process to integrate budget, enrollment considerations, and cost of instruction. (CFR 2.4, 3.4, 4.1, 4.5, 4.8) 2. Develop and implement decision-making processes that are transparent, inclusive, and place a priority on two-way communication and shared governance. (CFR 1.7, 3.11, 4.6, 4.8) 3. Design and implement leadership development and succession pathways to ensure the institution has sufficient and qualified leadership capacity at all levels. (CFR 3.9) 4. Evaluate and modify existing workgroups and initiatives to ensure clarity of objectives, to eliminate redundancies, to support broad campus understanding and success, and to foster collaboration across divisions. (CFR 1.7, 4.1, 4.5) 2 5. Review and adjust workload expectations to prevent burnout and ensure that individuals filling multiple roles can effectively contribute to institutional priorities. (CFR 2.14, 3.2, 3.9) 6. Develop and implement plans to address the climate concerns of faculty, staff, administrators, and students. (CFRs 3.2, 4.3) 7. Focus on advancing post-graduation outcomes of all students to fully realize the institutional mission. (CFR 2.11) In accordance with Commission policy, a copy of this letter is being sent to the chair of California State University East Bay’s governing board. A copy of this letter is also being sent to Chancellor Garcia, California State University. The Commission expects that the team report and this action letter will be posted in a readily accessible location on the CSUEB website and widely distributed throughout the institution to promote further engagement and improvement and to support the institution's response to the specific issues identified in these documents. The team report and the Commission’s action letter will also be posted on the WSCUC website. If the institution wishes to respond to the Commission action on its own website, WSCUC will post a link to that response on the WSCUC website. Finally, the Commission wishes to express its appreciation for the extensive work that CSUEB undertook in preparing for and supporting this accreditation review. WSCUC is committed to an accreditation process that adds value to institutions while contributing to public accountability, and we thank you for your continued support of this process. Please contact me if you have any questions about this letter or the action of the Commission. Sincerely, A. Your comments were very helpful in informing the Commission’s deliberations. The date of this action constitutes the effective date of the institution’s status with WSCUC. The Commission acted to remove a Show Cause order and impose the sanction of Warning because, although the college has demonstrated compliance with several of the issues identified by the Commission, it found that SDCC has not demonstrated that it is in compliance with WSCUC Standard 3. SDCC has been on sanction since July of 2019, which is outside the maximum time for compliance with Commission standards. Since the Commission believes that forward progress has been and continues to be made in the area of financial sustainability and resource planning, the Commission acted to grant a good cause extension until spring 2025. At that time, the Commission will determine whether the institution has taken appropriate corrective action and come into compliance with the Standards. If the Commission determines that deficiencies remain, the Commission may take an “adverse action,” in this case the withdrawal of accreditation. Procedural History In a letter dated July 14, 2023, after a Special Visit in spring 2023, the Commission acted to withdraw SDCC’s accreditation because the institution had been continuously on sanction for a period of four years with no further extension of accreditation available under WSCUC policies. The action was subject to appeal. By letter of July 25, 2023, 1 SDCC submitted a Notice of Intent to Appeal the Commission’s Action. On September 22, 2023, SDCC submitted a request for the Commission to consider new evidence and the basis for that request. The New Evidence Panel directed the new evidence to be submitted to the Commission. In November 2023 the Commission accepted SDCC’s evidence of compliance with CFRs 2.10, 2.13, and 3.8, and found that while SDCC was not in compliance with CFR 3.4, the evidence demonstrated that there was a sufficient basis to grant SDCC a good cause extension of accreditation. 1 Accordingly, the Commission granted a good cause extension to July 30, 2024, and continued SDCC’s accreditation on the sanction of Show Cause. A Special Visit was scheduled for spring 2024 to review the institution’s compliance with Standard 3, specifically CFR 3.4. Actions 1. Receive the Special Visit team report that focused on financial sustainability, resource planning, enrollment management, and diversification of revenue sources 2. Remove an Order to Show Cause 3. Issue a Warning 4. Grant a good cause extension 5. Schedule an Interim Report to be submitted by March 1, 2025 to provide an update on financial sustainability. Warning Warning reflects the Commission’s finding that an institution fails to meet one or more of WSCUC Standards of accreditation. While on Warning, any new site or degree program initiated by the institution is regarded as a substantive change (see the Substantive Change Manual for details). The accredited status of the institution continues during the Warning period. The Commission action to issue a Warning is subject to Commission Review, described below. When the Commission finds that an institution fails to meet one or more of the Standards of accreditation, it is required to notify the institution of the deficiencies and establish a time period within which the deficiencies must be corrected, withdraw the institution’s accreditation, or extend the timeframe for good cause shown. An institution under sanction must address the areas cited by the Commission expeditiously, with seriousness and the full attention of the institution’s leadership. It is the responsibility of the institution to demonstrate to the Commission that it has understood the issues raised in this letter, responded to them satisfactorily, and has made the necessary changes to come into compliance with Standard 3. Resource planning and development include realistic budgeting, enrollment management, and diversification of revenue sources. A request by the institution for Commission review is limited to one or more of the four bases outlined in the 2013 Handbook of accreditation, Revised. If SDCC intends to seek review, the request, co-signed by the CEO and chair of the governing board, must be submitted to the president of the Commission within 28 days of the date of this letter together with the required fee. Commission policy requires that in the case of a sanction, a public statement will be prepared in consultation with the institution acknowledging the institution’s status. The Commission reserves the right to make the final determination of the nature and content of the public statement. The Commission expects that the team report and this action letter will be posted in a readily accessible location on the SDCC’s website and widely distributed throughout the institution to promote further engagement and improvement and to support the institution's response to the specific issues identified in these documents. The team report and the Commission’s action letter will also be posted on the WSCUC website. If the institution wishes to respond to the Commission action on its own website, WSCUC will post a link to that response on the WSCUC website. Finally, the Commission wishes to express its appreciation for the extensive work that SDCC undertook in preparing for and supporting this accreditation review. WSCUC is committed to an accreditation process that adds value to institutions while contributing to public accountability, and we thank you for your continued support of this process. Please contact me if you have any questions about this letter or the action of the Commission. Sincerely, Jamienne S. parsed_reason_text: July 11, 2025 Dr. Alanka Brown Chief Executive Officer and Dean California College - ASU 1111 South Broadway, Suite 100 Los Angeles, CA 09915 Dear Dr. Brown: This letter serves as formal notification and official record of action taken concerning California College - ASU (CC - ASU) by the WASC Senior College and University Commission (WSCUC) at its meeting June 27, 2025. At that meeting, the Commission acted to continue the sanction of Warning. This action was taken after consideration of the report of the review team that conducted the Special Visit to CC - ASU March 5 – 7, 2025 using the 2023 Standards of accreditation. The Commission also reviewed the institutional report and exhibits submitted by CC - ASU prior to the Special Visit, and the institution’s May 29, 2025 response to the team report. The Commission appreciated the opportunity to discuss the visit with you and your colleagues Christian Osmena, Chair of the CC – ASU Board of Trustees; Nancy Gonzales, Board of Trustees Member; Lisa Loo, Board of Trustees Member; and Darlene Gartrell, Board of Trustees Member. Your comments were very helpful in informing the Commission’s deliberations. The Commission acted to continue the sanction of Warning because, although the college had demonstrated improvement with some of the issues identified by the Commission, it found CC- ASU had not demonstrated that it is in compliance with WSCUC Standard 3. Under WSCUC policies, when the Commission finds that an institution fails to meet one or more of the Standards of accreditation, it is required to notify the institution of the deficiencies and establish a time period within which the deficiencies must be corrected (see the Procedural History below). CC – ASU has been on sanction since December 15, 2023. Institutions on Warning have up to two years from the date of action to correct the situation; CC – ASU has until December 15, 2025 to provide evidence of compliance with Standard 3. At that time, the Commission will determine whether the institution has taken appropriate corrective action and come into compliance with the Standards. If the Commission determines that deficiencies remain, the Commission may take an “adverse action,” in this case the withdrawal of accreditation, or if warranted grant a good cause extension of accreditation for no more than two additional years. Procedural History On July 12, 2021, the Commission reaffirmed CC – ASU’s accreditation for six years, issued a Notice of Concern (NOC), and scheduled a Special Visit for spring 2024. On December 20, 2022, the Commission approved a Change of Control to the Arizona Board of Regents on behalf of Arizona State University (ASU). Recommendations from that 2022 Structural Change approval were added to the scope of the spring 2024 Special Visit. Based on the findings of the post-implementation visit following the Change of Control, the Executive Committee removed the NOC and issued a Warning dated December 15, 2023. The compliance issues with Standard 3 that led to imposition of a Warning were also added to the focus of the spring 2024 Special Visit. The Commission determined that CC – ASU had not demonstrated compliance with Standard 3 and scheduled a Special Visit for spring 2025. Actions 1. Receive the Special Visit team report that focused on: non-compliance with Standard 3 including (1) financial sustainability, (2) student enrollment, (3) shared governance, and (4) facilities; and the following areas including (1) governing board effectiveness, (2) student success, (3) student support, (4) space to foster institutional identity and belonging for students, (5) faculty governance structures, and, (6) ALO support 2. Continue a Warning 3. Schedule a Progress Report to be submitted by November 1, 2025 to address: a. graduation rates for spring 2025. b. retention rates for first year to second year students for fall 2025. c. new student enrollment for fall 2025. d. audited financial statements for FY 2025; internally prepared financial statements for the third quarter of 2025 including a balance sheet, income statement and year-to-date budget to actual analysis; an analysis of projected v. actual enrollments for the fall 2025 term; and a three to five year disaggregated financial forecast. e. a statement reflecting the sole member’s annual commitments including financial contributions and in-kind support. f. how financial information provided demonstrates the impact of corrective measures on the institution’s compliance with CFR 3.4 and 3.5 and, therefore, why a good cause extension of the institution’s accreditation is warranted under WSCUC policies and procedures (see the 2023 Handbook of accreditation on Commission Decisions on Institutions; Possible Commission Actions; Good Cause Extension). Warning Warning reflects the Commission’s finding that an institution fails to meet one or more of the WSCUC Standards of accreditation. While on Warning, any new site or degree program initiated by the institution is regarded as a substantive change (see the Substantive Change Manual for details). The accredited status of the institution continues during the Warning period. The Commission action to impose Warning is subject to Commission Review, described below. When the Commission finds that an institution fails to meet one or more of the Standards of accreditation, it is required to notify the institution of the deficiencies and establish a time period within which the deficiencies must be corrected. Under the Commission’s policies the timeframe may not exceed two years. If an institution has not remedied the deficiencies at the conclusion of this sanction period, the Commission is required to withdraw the institution’s accreditation or extend the timeframe for good cause shown. The initial extension may not exceed two years. An institution under sanction must address the areas cited by the Commission expeditiously, 2 with seriousness and the full attention of the institution’s leadership. It is the responsibility of the institution to demonstrate to the Commission that it has understood the issues raised in this letter, responded to them satisfactorily, and has made the necessary changes to come into compliance with Standard 3. It is the responsibility of the Commission to determine whether the institution has come into compliance with Standard 3. Non-Compliance with Standards: Deficiencies to be Addressed The Commission determined that CC – ASU has not demonstrated compliance with Standard 3, specifically CFRs 3.4 and 3.5: CFR 3.4 Resource planning and development include realistic budgeting, enrollment management, and diversification of revenue sources. Resource allocation is aligned with evidence-based educational and student success objectives consistent with operational and strategic planning. CFR 3.5 The institution is financially stable and has resources sufficient to ensure long-term sustainability. The institution has unqualified or unmodified independent financial audits. financial Sustainability (CFRs 3.4 and 3.5) CC – ASU is not financially stable. The college missed its enrollment target of new students for fall 2024 by 95%. CC – ASU will end the 2024-2025 academic year in deficit despite cost cutting implemented across the college and the on-going commitment of cash from ASU. The institution’s goal is to achieve at least a break-even budget by 2027-2028. While the college has recently implemented a budget strategy utilizing zero-based budgeting and including the campus community in financial discussions, further budget planning lacks specificity beyond targets for enrollment and tuition revenue growth. CC – ASU continues to have a negative financial composite score and remains on Heightened Cash Monitoring 1. The college must evidence that its financial planning and development is supporting and sustaining the resources needed to provide quality education and achieve successful student outcomes. Planning and development should articulate resources provided by the sole member to help anticipate costs the institution will have to assume once it achieves balanced budgets. Enrollment Management (CFR 3.4) CC - ASU enrolled three new students in fall 2024, compared with an enrollment goal of 59. Despite the shortfall, CC – ASU has set an aggressive enrollment goal of 79 new students for fall 2025. The plan for two-thirds of projected enrollment is from the institution’s liberal arts program, which currently has zero students enrolled, in part because it has not yet received approval for federal financial aid. Faculty indicated they were not aware of the plans for the targeted liberal arts program enrollment for fall 2025. CC – ASU recently switched to the Common Application as a part of its admissions process. Initial results included a significant number of incomplete applications and applicants that were either undecided about their emphasis or expressed interest in programs the institution doesn’t offer. 3 CC – ASU must develop and implement structures and processes and utilize appropriate data to grow student enrollment, including but not limited to strategies grounded in evidence of effectiveness, realistic multi-year enrollment projections, marketing, student support and financial planning and management. Areas for Development The Commission also requires the institution to respond to the following areas for development: 1. Improve utilization of retention and graduation measures to help identify effective enrollment strategies, including benchmarking against peer institutions. (CFRs 2.10, 4.2, 4.4) 2. Disseminate retention and graduation measures across all relevant constituencies to foster a deeper understanding of impact and the alignment of policies and practices to support student success. (CFRs 2.10, 4.2, 4.3, 4.5, 4.6) 3. Examine the extent to which the CC – ASU climate, including faculty and staff resources and support, promotes student success and use lessons learned to make appropriate changes. (CFRs 1.4, 1.5, 4.3) 4. Ensure that the ALO has adequate capacity, support, and resources to carry out all ALO responsibilities. (accreditation Liaison Officer Policy) Next Steps The Commission requires a meeting between the WSCUC staff and representatives of CC-ASU, including the Chief Executive Officer, representatives of the governing board, and senior faculty leadership, within 90 days from the date of this letter. The purposes of the meeting are to further clarify the reasons for the Commission’s findings and bases for decision, to review the actions taken as of the date of the meeting, and to discuss the institution’s plans for responding to this Commission action. WSCUC will contact CC-ASU’s ALO to make arrangements for this meeting. The Commission decision to continue the Warning is subject to Commission review. A request by the institution for Commission review is limited to the criteria outlined in the 2023 Handbook of accreditation. If CC-ASU intends to seek review, the request, co-signed by the CEO and chair of the governing board, must be submitted to the president of the Commission within 28 days of the date of this letter together with the required fee. Commission policy requires that in the case of a sanction, a public statement will be prepared in consultation with the institution acknowledging the institution’s status. The Commission reserves the right to make the final determination of the nature and content of the public statement. The institution must post the statement within seven business days, along with a copy of the Commission letter, in a readily accessible location on the institution’s website and accompanying every reference to WSCUC accreditation. The institution must also provide evidence to WSCUC that the public statement has been posted. 4 Enclosed is a copy of a sample public statement, which CC-ASU may use as it stands. If you wish to propose revisions to the sample, your proposed changes must be forwarded by email to Vice President Maloney within 24 hours of receipt of this letter. In addition, any reference to WSCUC accreditation on the website and in public statements must be accompanied by the words “Currently on Warning.” In accordance with Commission policy, a copy of this letter is being sent to the chair of CC- ASU’s governing board. The Commission expects that the team report and this action letter will be posted in a readily accessible location on the CC-ASU’s website and widely distributed throughout the institution to promote further engagement and improvement and to support the institution's response to the specific issues identified in these documents. The team report and the Commission’s action letter will also be posted on the WSCUC website within one business day of the date of this letter. If the institution wishes to respond to the Commission action on its own website, WSCUC will post a link to that response on the WSCUC website. Finally, the Commission wishes to express its appreciation for the institution’s preparation and support for this Special Visit review. WSCUC is committed to an accreditation process that adds value to institutions while contributing to public accountability, and we thank you for your continued support of this process. Please contact me if you have any questions about this letter or the action of the Commission. Sincerely, A. Warning reflects the Commission’s finding that an institution has significant issues of noncompliance with one or more of the WSCUC Standards of accreditation. The Commission has determined that CC - ASU is not in compliance with WSCUC Standard 3. When the Commission finds that an institution fails to meet one or more of the Standards of accreditation, it is required to notify the institution of these findings and give the institution a period of time to correct the deficiencies. Under the Commission’s policies the timeframe may not exceed two years from the initial Warning unless the institution presents evidence that there is good cause to provide further time for corrective measures and the Commission determines the evidence supports an extension of time. It is the responsibility of the Commission to determine, at the end of the sanction period, whether the institution has made the necessary corrections and has come into compliance with Commission Standards. The accredited status of CC - ASU continues during the Warning period and students’ status within the college is not affected by this sanction. CC – ASU has until December 15, 2025 to provide evidence of compliance with Standard 3. At that time, the Commission will determine whether the institution has taken appropriate corrective action and come into compliance with the Standards. If the Commission determines that deficiencies remain, the Commission may take an “adverse action,” in this case the withdrawal of accreditation, or if warranted grant a good cause extension of accreditation for no more than two additional years. The Commission’s decision to continue to impose a Warning on CC - ASU is subject to the terms and conditions contained in the Commission Action Letter dated June 27, 2025. This document is available on the WSCUC website. Anyone who has questions about CC - ASU’s accreditation status should contact Dr. Alanka Brown, accreditation Liaison Officer at CC - ASU. 6

At that meeting the Commission acted to continue Golden Gate University on Notice of Concern. This action was taken after consideration of the report of the review team that conducted the accreditation Visit to GGU April 9 – 11, 2025 using the 2023 Standards of accreditation. The Commission also reviewed the institutional report and exhibits submitted by GGU prior to the Offsite Review (OSR), the supplemental materials requested by the team after the OSR, and the institution’s June 10, 2025, response to the team report. The Commission appreciated the opportunity to discuss the visit with you and your colleagues Melinda Dunn, Board Chair; Rocco Lamana, Associate Vice President for Academic Affairs and ALO; and Elaine Clark, CFO. Your comments were very helpful in informing the Commission’s deliberations. The date of this action constitutes the effective date of the institution’s new status with WSCUC. The Commission has acted to extend the Notice of Concern. While GGU has been on Notice of Concern since July 2021, which typically extends beyond the general practice of four years for such notices, the Commission has determined this extension is warranted. The university has demonstrated compliance with all four Standards; however, further progress toward financial sustainability remains necessary. The Commission recognizes the significant improvements made while acknowledging that continued monitoring through a Notice of Concern is appropriate to ensure long-term institutional stability. Actions 1. Receive the accreditation Visit team report 2. Reaffirm accreditation for a period of six years 3. Continue the Notice of Concern 4. Schedule the next reaffirmation review with the Offsite Review in fall 2030 and the accreditation Visit in spring 2031 5. Schedule a Special Visit in spring 2027 to provide an update on financial sustainability, as outlined in the five requirements requiring a response Commendations The Commission commends the institution for: 1. Forging strategic partnerships to extend educational reach through regional collaborations and cohort-based initiatives. 2. A culture of belonging that authentically embodies the university's core mission and values, inspiring meaningful engagement and shared purpose across the campus community. 3. Championing student success through responsive, timely support services that effectively address diverse learner needs, enhancing both satisfaction and sense of community. 4. Drawing upon collegial faculty who care deeply about students, demonstrate a steadfast commitment to the mission, and prioritize student academic success. Notice of Concern A Notice of Concern provides notice to the institution that, while it currently meets WSCUC Standards, it is in danger of being found out of compliance with one or more Standards if current trends or findings continue. Institutions issued a Notice of Concern are scheduled for a Special Visit. If the issues are not addressed, a sanction could be imposed as described in the 2023 Handbook of accreditation. A Notice of Concern is public information and will be posted on the WSCUC website. Standard at Risk of Non-Compliance and Requiring a Response GGU is at risk of non-compliance with Standard 3 (CFRs 3.4, 3.5). The university faces concerning financial challenges: limited cash flow affecting operational flexibility, recurring operating deficits impacting financial stability, and revenue uncertainty creating vulnerability. While a comprehensive financial recovery plan has been developed, these interconnected issues present challenges to the university's fiscal health. The Commission requires GGU to: 1. Continue to move forward with the real estate transactions to reduce the institution’s facility costs and eliminate long-term debt. (CFRs 3.4, 3.5) 2. Strengthen fiscal monitoring and expense controls, pursue enrollment revenue diversification strategies, track projected enrollment targets and budget projections against actual performance, address the multi-year deficit, and employ financial discipline for long-term sustainability. (CFRs 3.4, 3.5) 3. Given the anticipated liquidity needs, continue to closely forecast cash balances to ensure that spending does not outpace the realization of new revenues. (CFRs 3.4, 3.5) 4. Enhance the advancement function to develop a comprehensive donor engagement strategy spanning all constituent groups to maximize philanthropic support. (CFRs 3.4, 3.5) 5. Enhance financial reporting systems for the Board of Trustees to provide comprehensive, timely, and easily interpretable fiscal data, enabling Trustees to exercise more informed oversight. (CFRs 3.4, 3.10) Areas for Development The Commission also requires the institution to respond to the following areas for development: 2 1. Clarify the presidential selection process (e.g., search firms, stakeholder involvement, timelines, milestones and progress) to all campus constituents. (CFRs 1.7, 3.1, 3.9) 2. Continue to build a culture of trust, respect, and transparent communication with all stakeholders and constituents, creating secure channels that allow for the safe expression of concerns. (CFRs 1.3, 1.8, 3.7, 4.5) 3. Recruit trustees in sufficient numbers, with diverse backgrounds, expertise, and competencies, thereby distributing governance responsibilities while strengthening oversight and strategic decision-making capacity. (CFRs 1.8, 3.8) 4. Uphold accreditation standards for all distance education offerings, including GGU Worldwide, by ensuring compliance with the credit hour policy, maintaining substantive faculty-initiated student interaction, and adhering to WSCUC Agreements with Unaccredited Entities policy. (CFRs 1.4, 1.8, 3.11) Next Steps In accordance with Commission policy, a copy of this letter is being sent to the chair of GGU’s governing board. The Commission expects that the team report and this action letter will be posted in a readily accessible location on the GGU website and widely distributed throughout the institution to promote further engagement and improvement and to support the institution's response to the specific issues identified in these documents. The team report and the Commission’s action letter will also be posted on the WSCUC website. If the institution wishes to respond to the Commission action on its own website, WSCUC will post a link to that response on the WSCUC website. Finally, the Commission wishes to express its appreciation for the extensive work that Golden Gate University undertook in preparing for and supporting this accreditation review. WSCUC is committed to an accreditation process that adds value to institutions while contributing to public accountability, and we thank you for your continued support of this process. Please contact me if you have any questions about this letter or the action of the Commission. Sincerely, A. Florida Memorial University remains an accredited member of the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges while on the sanction of Probation for Good Cause. If an institution has not demonstrated compliance with all the standards of the Principles of accreditation at the conclusion of its two-year maximum monitoring period, the SACSCOC Board of Trustees must (1) remove the institution from membership or (2) continue accreditation for Good Cause. Action by SACSCOC Board of Trustees took place on December 8, 2024, and the institution’s next review is December 2025. What is the accreditation status of Georgetown College? Georgetown College is accredited by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges. Following the December 2024 action of the Board, the institution was denied reaffirmation, continued in accreditation, and placed on Probation for Good Cause for twelve (12) months following SACSCOC Board action taken in December 2022 on its comprehensive decennial review. SACSCOC accreditation includes all components of the institution—all programs, branch campuses, off-campus sites, and distance education programs as reported to SACSCOC; thus, the status of Probation for Good Cause applies to the entire institution. What does it mean to be denied reaffirmation, continued in accreditation, and placed on Probation for Good Cause? Georgetown College had been on monitoring for two (2) years and the maximum consecutive time for a monitoring period is two (2) years. Georgetown College was at the end of its two-year monitoring period in December 2024, however, instead of removing the institution’s accreditation, the SACSCOC Board of Trustees can extend accreditation for Good Cause if (1) the institution has demonstrated significant recent accomplishments in addressing non-compliance, and (2) the institution has provided evidence which makes it reasonable for the Board to assume it will remedy all deficiencies within a 12–month period, and (3) the institution has provided assurance to the Board that it is not aware of any other reasons, other than those identified by the Board, why the institution cannot be continued for Good Cause. Probation is the most serious public sanction imposed by the SACSCOC Board of Trustees short of loss of accreditation. In December 2025, Georgetown College will have been on Probation for Good Cause for one (1) year. A Special Committee was authorized to visit the institution. These standards expect an institution to: 1) have a governing board of at least five members that (b) exercises fiduciary oversight of the institution; 2) Have sound financial resources and a demonstrated, stable financial base to support the mission of the institution and the scope of its programs and services; and 3) Manage its financial resources in a responsible manner. SACSCOC staff will not speculate on what decision might be made by the Board of Trustees in December 2025. On August 18, 2025, SACSCOC received litigation documents from Saint Augustine’s University confirming that SAU was granted a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction by the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia Atlanta Division. The order requires that SACSCOC reinstate the institution’s accreditation status (accredited on Probation) pending the outcome of litigation. Accordingly, the institution’s accreditation status has been reinstated as of August 18, 2025 and will remain in place for the duration of the current legal process. NOTE: The following chronology is included to provide a history of the accreditation process for the institution. For additional information regarding the SACSCOC accreditation process, access the Principles of accreditation: Foundations for Quality Enhancement. On December 3, 2023, the SACSCOC Board of Trustees removed Saint Augustine’s University from membership as an accredited institution; however, the institution remained accredited and on Probation during the 10-day time period after receipt of official notification in which it can submit a formal appeal. The institution submitted its formal request to appeal the decision of the Board on January 19, 2024, and maintained its status of accreditation on Probation pending the decision of the Appeals Committee. On February 27, 2024, the SACSCOC Appeals Committee of the College Delegate Assembly unanimously affirmed the December 3, 2023, decision of the SACSCOC Board of Trustees to terminate the accreditation of Saint Augustine’s University, Raleigh, North Carolina. The Appeals Committee found the SACSCOC Board of Trustees’ decision to be reasonable, not arbitrary, and based on the standards cited. “Specifically, the Appeals Committee found the Board’s decision reflected a reasonable application of the Principles of accreditation: Foundations for Quality Enhancement (“Principles”), which clearly included the use of appropriate professional judgment of evaluators representing SACSCOC in the assessment of compliance with the following core requirements and standards of the Principles: Core Requirement 4.1 (Governing board characteristics), Core Requirement 13.1 (financial resources), Core Requirement 13.2 (financial documents), Standard 13.3 (financial responsibility), Standard 13.4 (Control of finances), and Standard 13.6 (Federal and state responsibilities).” Further, the Appeals Committee found that the institution failed to meet the provisions of Good Cause. Pursuant to 34 CFR Section 602.20(e) and 20 U.S.C. 1099b(e), the institution agreed to submit any dispute involving the final denial, withdrawal, or termination of accreditation to initial arbitration prior to any other legal action. On March 8, 2024, Saint Augustine’s University notified the SACSCOC President of its intent to pursue arbitration of the Appeals Committee decision. SACSCOC acknowledged receipt of the notice, and the arbitration process commenced in accordance with the Arbitration of Adverse Actions policy statement. The institution remained accredited on Probation during the arbitration process. On July 21, 2024, SACSCOC and Saint Augustine’s University (SAU) were notified of the decision of the panel of arbitrators. In a unanimous decision, the panel reversed the decision of the SACSCOC Appeals Committee of the College Delegate Assembly. Saint Augustine’s University remained an accredited institution on Probation for Good Cause. In December 2024, the Committees on Compliance and Reports (C&R) reviewed the remand from the July 21, 2024 arbitration decision. The Committee reviewed the institution’s ongoing compliance with the aforementioned standards. On December 8, 2024, the Board of Trustees voted to remove SAU from membership. The institution remained 1 accredited and on Probation for Good Cause for ten (10) days following the decision and pending receipt of official notification of its intent to appeal. On January 24, 2025, Saint Augustine’s University notified the President of SACSCOC of its request to appeal the December 8, 2024 action of the SACSCOC Board of Trustees removing the institution from membership, which secured the institution’s status of accreditation on Probation for Good Cause pending the decision of the Appeals Committee. On February 27, 2025, the Appeals Committee of the College Delegate Assembly convened in Atlanta, Georgia. In accordance with SACSCOC policy and procedure, representatives of Saint Augustine’s University presented new and verifiable financial information material to the Board’s adverse decision as evidence of grounds for the adverse action to be remanded to the Board. Following the hearing, the Appeals Committee deliberated and had seven (7) days to provide its decision in writing to Saint Augustine’s University and the President of SACSCOC. On March 5, 2025, the Appeals Committee of the College Delegate Assembly unanimously affirmed the December 8, 2024, decision of the SACSCOC Board of Trustees to remove SAU from membership. The Appeals Committee found the SACSCOC Board of Trustees’ decision to be reasonable, not arbitrary, and based on the standards cited. “Specifically, the Appeals Committee found the Board’s decision reflected a reasonable application of the Principles of accreditation: Foundations for Quality Enhancement (“Principles”), which clearly included the use of appropriate professional judgment of evaluators representing SACSCOC in the assessment of compliance with the following core requirements and standards of the Principles: Core Requirement 4.1 (Governing board characteristics), Core Requirement 13.1 (financial resources), Core Requirement 13.2 (financial documents), Standard 13.3 (financial responsibility), Standard 13.4 (Control of finances), Standard 13.5 (Control of sponsored research/external funds) and Standard 13.6 (Federal and state responsibilities). Pursuant to 34 CFR Section 602.20(e) and 20 U.S.C. 1099b( e), the institution agreed to submit any dispute involving the final denial, withdrawal, or termination of accreditation to initial arbitration prior to any other legal action. SACSCOC policy, Arbitration of Adverse Actions, the institution’s Chief Executive Officer may submit in writing to the President of SACSCOC by electronic transmission within ten (10) calendar days of the institution’s receipt of the final written decision of the Appeals Committee. On March 14, 2025, Saint Augustine’s University notified the SACSCOC President of its intent to pursue arbitration of the Appeals Committee decision. SACSCOC acknowledged receipt of this notice, and the arbitration process commenced on April 16, 2025. The institution remained accredited on Probation for Good Cause during the arbitration process. On June 26, 2025, the Saint Augustine’s University (SAU) arbitration hearing took place in Atlanta, Georgia. Representatives of SAU presented the university’s request to amend or remand the decision of the Appeals Committee. On July 14, 2025, SACSCOC and SAU received the written decision of the panel of arbitrators. In a unanimous decision, the panel affirmed the decision of the SACSCOC Appeals Committee of the College Delegate Assembly. parsed_reason_text: November 25, 2024 Mr. John Pullo President Keystone College One College Green La Plume, PA 18440-0200 Notification of Adverse Action Dear Mr. Pullo: On behalf of the Middle States Commission on Higher Education, I am writing to inform you that on November 21, 2024, the Commission acted as follows: To acknowledge receipt of the show cause report, submitted on August 1, 2024. To note the Commission actions of November 1, 2024. To note the on-site show cause visit by Commission representatives to the main campus at One College Green, La Plume, PA 18440 on August 27-28, 2024. To acknowledge receipt of the institution's intent to appear before the Commission to present its reasons why its accreditation should not be withdrawn. To note the presentation by the institution's representatives on November 20, 2024. To acknowledge receipt of the institution's request to present new information as approved by the Chair of the Commission: (1) letter of submission, (2) summary and evidence, and (3) a presentation for use during the show cause appearance. To withdraw accreditation from Keystone College effective December 31, 2024. The institution failed to (1) provide evidence that demonstrates compliance with Commission standards for accreditation (Standard II, Ethics and Integrity; Standard VI, Planning, resources, and Institutional Improvement; and Standard VII, Governance, Leadership, and Administration), policies and procedures, and applicable federal regulatory requirements; (2) demonstrate the capacity to make required improvements; and (3) demonstrate that it can sustain itself in the short or long term (accreditation Actions Policy and Procedures). The institution failed to provide evidence of compliance with (1) all applicable government laws and regulations (Standard II); (2) documented financial resources, funding base, and plans for financial development adequate to support its educational purposes and programs and to ensure financial stability (Standard VI); (3) a record of responsible fiscal management, including preparing a multi-year budget (Standard VI); (4) program responsibilities under existing federal title IV and other state laws and regulations, including any audits of financial aid programs as required by federal and state regulations (Standard II and Standard VI); (5) a governing body that serves the public interest, ensures that the institution clearly states and fulfills its mission and goals, has fiduciary responsibility for the institution, and is ultimately accountable for the academic quality, integrity, planning, and fiscal well-being of the institution (Standard VII); and (6) a governing body that plays a basic policy-making role in financial affairs to ensure integrity and strong financial management, including but not limited to timely review of audited financial statements and other documents related to the fiscal viability of the institution (Standard VII). This decision is based on the record before the Commission at the show cause appearance including: (1) a complex substantive change request submitted on September 1, 2023, for a change in legal status, form of control, or ownership and the institution's subsequent request on March 8, 2024, to withdraw the complex substantive change request, which was withdrawn by the Commission on April 4, 2024; (2) a self-study report submitted on February 1, 2024, the report of a subsequent visit by Commission representatives on March 17-20, 2024, and the institutional response; (3) a supplemental information report and teach-out plan and agreements submitted on April 12, 2024; (4) a substantive change request for institutional closure submitted on April 17, 2024, and the institution's subsequent request of September 6, 2024, to withdraw the request for institutional closure; (5) a supplemental information report and updated teach-out plan and agreements submitted on May 15, 2024; (6) a show cause report and teach-out plan and agreements submitted on August 1, 2024, the report of a subsequent visit by Commission representatives on August 27-28, 2024, and the institutional response; (7) information submitted by the institution on November 13, 2024, including new information submitted for the show cause appearance; and (8) a show cause appearance of institutional representatives on November 20, 2024. To approve the teach-out plan and teach-out agreements, requested by the Commission action of April 4, 2024, and to direct its implementation. To require an updated teach-out plan and teach-out agreements, due December 6, 2024, based on the adverse action to withdraw accreditation. To require a supplemental information report, due December 6, 2024, providing evidence of (1) executed teach-out agreements; (2) implementation of the teach-out plan; (3) completed and issued transcripts for any students wishing to transfer to another institution; (4) appropriate arrangements for the permanent disposition of student records so that students and alumni will be able to obtain accurate and complete transcripts in the future (Teach-Out Plans and Agreements Policy and Procedures); and (5) notifications and public disclosures. To direct the institution to immediately (1) notify all constituents of the withdrawal of accreditation, effective December 31, 2024; (2) notify the Keystone College community, including all governing board members, students, faculty, staff, and others with significant roles, of the status of the institution; and (3) provide accurate information regarding the institution's accreditation status with MSCHE on its website and wherever accreditation is referenced on the institution's web pages, publications, announcements, and in all other appropriate places and venues (Public Disclosures Policy and Procedures). To note this action is an adverse action subject to appeal in accordance with the Commission’s Appeals from Adverse Actions Procedures. The institution retains its Accredited status until the completion of any appeal. An explanation of this type of action is provided in the Commission's accreditation Actions Policy and Procedures. To note all final adverse actions are subject to the arbitration requirements in the Commission's Arbitration of Disputes Concerning Final Adverse Actions Procedures and federal regulation 34 CFR § 602.20(e). To note that the following conditions are in effect in the event of an appeal: (1) the institution does not enroll new students; (2) the institution does not market to or recruit new students; (3) the institution maintains a clear and accurate statement about its accreditation phase and accreditation status for the public on its website in accordance with the Commission's Public Disclosures Policy and Procedures (Appeals from Adverse Actions Procedures); (4) the institution has an approved teach-out plan with signed teach- out agreements and is implementing it according to that approval (Teach-Out Plan and Agreements Policy and Procedures); and (5) the institution remains operational with students actively enrolled in its degree-granting programs, is not facing imminent closure, and does not close. To note that if the Commission determines that the institution has violated any of the conditions listed above or any other of the Commission policies and procedures, standards for accreditation, requirements of affiliation, or federal regulations, the Commission will take additional action (Appeals from Adverse Actions Procedures); the institution forfeits its appellate rights; and the Commission reserves the right to take a final adverse action which is no longer subject to appeal. The Commission will revise the effective date that accreditation will cease as necessary. To note that the institution’s request, dated September 6, 2024, to proceed with a complex substantive change while on non-compliance show cause (Complex Substantive Change Procedures Section III.D) is no longer under consideration by the Executive Committee due to the Commission's adverse action to withdraw accreditation. The teach-out plan must be submitted in accordance with the Commission’s Teach-Out Plans and Agreements Policy and Procedures. The purpose of a teach-out plan is to provide a written plan that accounts for the equitable treatment of students if an institution, or an institutional location, ceases to operate before all students have completed their program of study. The teach-out plan must include signed teach-out agreements. To have its accreditation reaffirmed, an institution placed in a non-compliance status must demonstrate that it meets or continues to meet the standards for accreditation, requirements of affiliation, policies and procedures, and federal requirements. The Commission has determined that the institution could not demonstrate compliance in the areas indicated in the Commission’s action. Further, the history of the institution has been reported on the Statement of accreditation Status, which is available online at www.msche.org. Information presented below is in accord with SACSCOC’s disclosure policy; SACSCOC staff cannot comment further on questions specifically related to LeTourneau University. The institution has reviewed this statement prior to public posting. Action by SACSCOC Board of Trustees took place on June 15, 2023, and the institution’s next review is June 2024. What is the accreditation status of LeTourneau University? LeTourneau University is accredited by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges; however, the institution continued in accreditation and placed on Warning after review of a Referral Report regarding full-time faculty and program faculty. SACSCOC accreditation includes all components of the institution—all programs, branch campuses, off-campus sites, and distance learning programs as reported to SACSCOC; thus, the Warning status applies to the entire institution. What does it mean to be continued in accreditation and placed on Warning? Warning imposed by the SACSCOC Board of Trustees follows a determination of significant non-compliance with the Core Requirements or Standards of the Principles of accreditation, the accreditation standards of SACSCOC; failure to make timely and significant progress toward correcting the deficiencies that led to the findings of non-compliance; or failure to comply with SACSCOC policies and procedures. The maximum total time during a monitoring period that an institution may be on Warning is two years. In June 2024, LeTourneau University will have been on Warning for twelve (12) months. For additional information about sanctions, see the SACSCOC policy entitled “Sanctions. Denial of Reaffirmation, and Removal from Membership.” Why was LeTourneau University placed on Warning? LeTourneau University was continued in accreditation and placed on Warning because the SACSCOC Board of Trustees determined that the institution had failed to demonstrate compliance with Core Requirement 6.1 (Full-time faculty) and Standard 6.2.b (Program faculty). These standards expect the institution to (1) employ an adequate number of full-time faculty members to support the mission and goals of the institution; and (2) employ a sufficient number of full-time faculty members for each of its educational programs to ensure curriculum and program quality, integrity, and review. (To read the full statements for the standards cited above, access the Principles of accreditation: Foundations for Quality Enhancement.) What will happen in June 2024? The SACSCOC Board of Trustees will consider the accreditation status of LeTourneau University following a review of a Monitoring Report submitted by the institution addressing the standards cited above for non-compliance. The Board will have the following options: (1) remove the institution from Warning without an additional report; (2) remove the institution from Warning and request a Fifth-Year Follow-Up Report; (3) continue accreditation, continue the institution on Warning, request a Monitoring Report, with or without a Special Committee authorized, (4) continue accreditation, place the institution on Probation, request a Monitoring Report, and authorize a Special Committee; or (5) remove the institution from membership for failure to comply with the Principles of accreditation. SACSCOC staff will not speculate on what decision might be made by the Board of Trustees in June 2024. For additional information regarding SACSCOC’s accreditation process, access the Principles of accreditation: Foundations for Quality Enhancement. T

Information presented below is in accord with SACSCOC’s disclosure policy; SACSCOC staff cannot comment further on questions specifically related to Southwestern Adventist University. The institution has reviewed this statement prior to public posting. Action by SACSCOC Board of Trustees took place on June 15, 2023, and the institution’s next review is June 2024. What is the accreditation status of Southwestern Adventist University? Southwestern Adventist University is accredited by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges; however, the institution was continued in accreditation and placed on Warning after review of a Referral Report regarding student achievement, program faculty, and student outcomes for educational programs. SACSCOC accreditation includes all components of the institution—all programs, branch campuses, off- campus sites, and distance learning programs as reported to SACSCOC; thus, the Warning status applies to the entire institution. What does it mean to be continued in accreditation and placed on Warning? Warning imposed by the SACSCOC Board of Trustees follows a determination of significant non-compliance with the Core Requirements or Standards of the Principles of accreditation, the accreditation standards of SACSCOC; failure to make timely and significant progress toward correcting the deficiencies that led to the findings of non-compliance; or failure to comply with SACSCOC policies and procedures. The maximum total time during a monitoring period that an institution may be on Warning is two years. In June 2024, Southwestern Adventist University will have been on Warning for twelve (12) months. For additional information about sanctions, see the SACSCOC policy entitled “Sanctions, Denial of Reaffirmation, and Removal from Membership.” Why was Southwestern Adventist University placed on Warning? Southwestern Adventist University was continued in accreditation and placed on Warning because the SACSCOC Board of Trustees determined that the institution had failed to demonstrate compliance with Core Requirement 8.1 (Student achievement), Standard 6.2.b (Program faculty) and Standard 8.2.a (Student outcomes: educational programs). These standards expect the institution: (1) to identify, evaluate, and publish goals and outcomes for student achievement appropriate to the institution’s mission, the nature of the students it serves, and the kinds of programs offered. Further, this standard expects an institution to use multiple measures to document student success; (2) to employ a sufficient number of full-time faculty members for each of its educational programs to ensure curriculum and program quality, integrity, and review; and (3) to identify expected student learning outcomes, assess the extent to which it achieves these outcomes, and provide evidence of seeking improvement based on analysis of the results for each of its educational programs. (To read the full statements for the standards cited above, access the Principles of accreditation: Foundations for Quality Enhancement.) What will happen in June 2024? The SACSCOC Board of Trustees will consider the accreditation status of Southwestern Adventist University following a review of a Monitoring Report submitted by the institution addressing the standards cited above for non- compliance. The Board will have the following options: (1) remove the institution from Warning without an additional report; (2) remove the institution from Warning and request a Fifth-Year Follow-Up Report; (3) continue accreditation, continue the institution on Warning, request a Monitoring Report, with or without a Special Committee authorized; (4) continue accreditation, place the institution on Probation, request a Monitoring Report, and authorize a Special Committee; or (5) remove the institution from membership for failure to comply with the Principles of accreditation. SACSCOC staff will not speculate on what decision might be made by the Board of Trustees in June 2024. For additional information regarding SACSCOC’s accreditation process, access the Principles of accreditation: Foundations for Quality Enhancement.

parsed_reason_text: Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges (SACSCOC) http://www.sacscoc.org Disclosure Statement Regarding the Status of THE UNIVERSITY OF TEXAS AT EL PASO El Paso, Texas Issued June 23, 2023, by SACSCOC The following publicly available information is provided by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges (SACSCOC) concerning the accreditation of The University of Texas at El Paso. Information presented below is in accord with SACSCOC’s disclosure policy; SACSCOC staff cannot comment further on questions specifically related to The University of Texas at El Paso. The institution has reviewed this statement prior to public posting. Action by SACSCOC Board of Trustees took place on June 15, 2023, and the institution’s next review is December 2023. What is the accreditation status of The University of Texas at El Paso? The University of Texas at El Paso is accredited by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges; however, the institution continued in accreditation and placed on Warning after review of a Referral Report. SACSCOC accreditation includes all components of the institution—all programs, branch campuses, off-campus sites, and distance learning programs as reported to SACSCOC; thus, the Warning status applies to the entire institution. What does it mean to be continued in accreditation and placed on Warning? Warning imposed by the SACSCOC Board of Trustees follows a determination of significant non-compliance with the Core Requirements or Standards of the Principles of accreditation, the accreditation standards of SACSCOC; failure to make timely and significant progress toward correcting the deficiencies that led to the findings of non-compliance; or failure to comply with SACSCOC policies and procedures. The maximum total time during a monitoring period that an institution may be on Warning is two years. In December 2023, The University of Texas at El Paso will have been on Warning for six (6) months. For additional information about sanctions, see the SACSCOC policy entitled “Sanctions, Denial of Reaffirmation, and Removal from Membership.” Why was The University of Texas at El Paso placed on Warning? The University of Texas at El Paso was continued in accreditation and placed on Warning because the SACSCOC Board of Trustees determined that the institution had failed to demonstrate compliance with Core Requirement 6.1 (Full-time faculty), Core Requirement 9.2 (Program length), Standard 5.4 (Qualified administrative/academic officers), Standard 6.2.b (Program faculty) and Standard 6.2.c (Program coordination). These standards expect the institution to (1) employ an adequate number of full-time faculty members to support the mission and goals of the institution; (2) to offer one or more degree programs based on at least 60 semester credit hours or the equivalent at the associate level; at least 120 semester credit hours or the equivalent at the baccalaureate level; or at least 30 semester credit hours or the equivalent at the post-baccalaureate, graduate, or professional level. Further, this standard expects an institution to provide an explanation of equivalencies when using units other than semester credit hours and provide an appropriate justification for all degree programs and combined degree programs that include fewer than the required number of semester credit hours or its equivalent unit; (3) employ administrative and academic officers with appropriate experience and qualifications to lead the institution. Further, this standard expects an institution to evaluate those administrative and academic officers regularly; (4) employ a sufficient number of full- time faculty members for each of its educational programs to ensure curriculum and program quality, integrity, and review; and (5) assign appropriate responsibility for program coordination for each of its educational programs. (To read the full statements for the standards cited above, access the Principles of accreditation: Foundations for Quality Enhancement.) What will happen in December 2023? The SACSCOC Board of Trustees will consider the accreditation status of The University of Texas at El Paso following a review of a Monitoring Report submitted by the institution addressing the standards cited above for non- compliance. The Board will have the following options: (1) remove the institution from Warning without an additional report; (2) remove the institution from Warning and request a Fifth-Year Follow-Up Report; (3) continue accreditation, continue the institution on Warning, request a Monitoring Report, with or without a Special Committee authorized, (4) continue accreditation, place the institution on Probation, request a Monitoring Report, and authorize a Special Committee; or (5) remove the institution from membership for failure to comply with the Principles of accreditation. SACSCOC staff will not speculate on what decision might be made by the Board of Trustees in December 2023. For additional information regarding SACSCOC’s accreditation process, access the Principles of accreditation: Foundations for Quality Enhancement.

Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges (SACSCOC) http://www.sacscoc.org Disclosure Statement Regarding the Status of Marymount University Arlington, VA Issued June 26, 2025, by SACSCOC The following publicly available information is provided by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges (SACSCOC) concerning the accreditation of Marymount University. The information presented below is in accord with SACSCOC’s disclosure policy; SACSCOC staff cannot comment further on questions specifically related to Marymount University. The institution has reviewed this statement prior to public posting. Action by SACSCOC Board of Trustees took place on June 12, 2025, and the institution’s next review is June 2026. What is the accreditation status of Marymount University? Marymount University is accredited by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges. The institution was continued in accreditation and placed on Warning following the Board’s review of a Referral Report following submission of the institution’s Fifth-Year Interim Report in March 2024. SACSCOC accreditation includes all components of the institution—all programs, branch campuses, off-campus sites, and distance learning programs as reported to SACSCOC; thus, the Warning status applies to the entire institution. What does it mean to be continued in accreditation and placed on Warning? Warning imposed by the SACSCOC Board of Trustees follows a determination of significant non-compliance with the Core Requirements or Standards of the Principles of accreditation, the accreditation standards of SACSCOC; failure to make timely and significant progress toward correcting the deficiencies that led to the findings of non-compliance; or failure to comply with SACSCOC policies and procedures. An institution placed or continued on Warning remains in accredited status while on sanction. The maximum total time during a monitoring period that an institution may be on Warning is two years. In June 2026, Marymount University will have been on Warning for one year. For additional information about monitoring periods and sanctions, see the SACSCOC policy entitled Sanctions, Denial of Reaffirmation, and Removal from Membership. Why was Marymount University placed on Warning? Marymount University was continued in accreditation and placed on Warning because the SACSCOC Board of Trustees determined that the institution has not yet demonstrated compliance with Core Requirement 13.1 (financial resources), Standard 13.3 (financial responsibility), Standard 13.4 (Control of finances), and Standard 13.6 (Federal and state responsibilities) of the Principles of accreditation. These standards expect the institution to have sound financial resources and a demonstrated, stable financial base to support the mission of the institution and the scope of its programs and services; to manage its financial resources and operate in a fiscally responsible manner; to exercise appropriate control over all its financial resources; and that an institution (a) is in compliance with its program responsibilities under Title IV of the most recent Higher Education Act as amended and (b) audits financial aid programs as required by federal and state regulations. A Special Committee was not authorized to visit the institution. To read the full statements for the standards cited above, access the Principles of accreditation: Foundations for Quality Enhancement. What will happen in June 2026? The SACSCOC Board of Trustees will consider the accreditation status of Marymount University following the institution’s submission addressing the standard cited above for non-compliance. The Board will have the following options: (1) remove the institution from Warning without an additional report; (2) remove the institution from Warning and request a Follow-Up Report; (3) continue accreditation, continue the institution on Warning, and request a Second Monitoring Report, with or without a Special Committee authorized; (4) continue accreditation, place the institution on Probation, and request a Second Monitoring Report with or without a Special Committee authorized or (5) remove the institution from membership for failure to comply with the Principles of accreditation. SACSCOC staff will not speculate on what decision might be made by the Board of Trustees in June 2026. For additional information regarding SACSCOC’s accreditation process, please access our webpage at www.sacscoc.org. Comment: Marymount University

Virginia Union University is accredited by the Southern Association of Colleges and Schools Commission on Colleges and was placed on Warning. SACSCOC accreditation includes all components of the institution—all programs, branch campuses, off-campus sites, and distance education programs as reported to SACSCOC; thus, the Warning status applies to the entire institution. What does it mean to be continued in accreditation and placed on Warning? A Warning imposed by the SACSCOC Board of Trustees follows a determination of significant non-compliance with the Core Requirements or Standards of the Principles of accreditation, the accreditation standards of SACSCOC; failure to make timely and significant progress toward correcting the deficiencies that led to the findings of non-compliance; or failure to comply with SACSCOC policies and procedures. The maximum total time during a monitoring period that an institution may be on sanction is two years. In December 2023, Virginia Union University will have been on Warning for one (1) year. For additional information about sanctions, see the SACSCOC policy entitled “Sanctions, Denial of Reaffirmation, and Removal from Membership.” Why was Virginia Union University continued in accreditation and placed on Warning? Virginia Union University was continued in accreditation and placed on Warning because the SACSCOC Board of Trustees determined that the institution failed to demonstrate compliance with the Principles of accreditation, namely, Core Requirement 4.1 (Governing board characteristics), Core Requirement 13.2 (financial documents), Standard 7.3 (Administrative effectiveness), Standard 8.2.a (Student outcomes: educational programs), Standard 8.2.c (Student outcomes: academic and student services), Standard 13.3 (financial responsibility), Standard 13.4 (Control of finances), and Standard 13.6 (Federal and state responsibilities). A Special Committee was not authorized to visit the institution. (To read the full statements for the standards cited above, access the Principles of accreditation: Foundation for Quality Enhancement.) (To read the full statements for the standards cited above, access the Principles of accreditation: Foundation for Quality Enhancement.) What will happen in December 2023? The SACSCOC Board of Trustees will consider the accreditation status of Virginia Union University following a review of a Monitoring Report submitted by the institution addressing the standards cited above. The Board will have the following options: (1) remove the institution from Warning without an additional report; (2) remove from Warning and request a Follow-Up Report at the time of the submission of the Fifth- Year Interim Report; (3) continue accreditation for Good Cause, place the institution on Probation, request a Monitoring Report, and authorize a Special Committee; or (4) remove the institution from membership for failure to comply with the Principles of accreditation. SACSCOC staff will not speculate on what decision might be made by the Board of Trustees in December 2023. For additional information regarding SACSCOC’s accreditation process, access the Principles of accreditation: Foundation for Quality Enhancement.
